newsitem.title: USA: Archer tax plan closes some corporate loopholes.
newsitem.headline: Archer tax plan closes some corporate loopholes.

text.p: House Ways and Means Committee chairman Bill Archer's tax plan released on Monday included some provisions designed to close favored corporate and investor tax avoidance strategies.

The single largest revenue raiser among these provisions, adding more than $1.6 billion over five years to federal coffers, would eliminate a popular technique used in mergers and acquisitions known as a "Morris Trust."
Using a trust, corporations have been allowed to spin-off tax-free to their shareholders units of companies they acquire.
Many companies have complained that the April 16, 1997, effective date in the Archer plan and earlier proposals would hamper acquisitions already underway.

The plan would also raise $708 million over five years by taxing investors who sell short stock that they own. Known as "shorting against the box," the technique allows an investor to effectively sell a stock holding without triggering capital gains taxes.
Under the plan, taxes would be owed on transactions made after the plan is enacted or for deals dating back to January 12, 1996, that remain in place 30 days after enactment.
Archer's plan would raise $1.2 billion by limiting the use of corporate losses to offset taxes in previous years.

Under the plan, losses could be used to offset taxes from the previous two years, down from three under present law. Losses could be carried forward for 20 years, up from 15 under present law. The provisions take effect on losses generated in taxable years beginning after the plan is enacted.
Another provision would raise $74 million by limiting the corporate dividends received deduction that allows companies to avoid paying taxes on most dividends.
The Archer plan modifies the required holding period for all dividends "received or accrued" 30 days after the proposal is enacted.

Other provisions of the tax plan left lobbyists in Washington groping for more details. The Ways and Means Committee provided only short descriptions, saying fuller details would be released later in the day.

A move to deny interest deductions "on certain debt instruments" was expected to raise $148 million. A lobbyist said the provision might relate to mandatorily convertible bonds, debt securities with equity-like features.

Determination of original issue discount on "pooled debt obligations subject to acceleration" would raise $1.3 billion. A bank lobbyist feared the plank would alter the tax treatment of interest banks collect on credit cards.
